steps.title: Antichains and Permutation Counting
steps.prompt:
Let [n]={1,2,...,n}. A family F of subsets of [n] is an antichain if no two distinct members A,B of F satisfy A⊂B.

Prove the inequality

Σ_{A∈F} 1/C(n,|A|) ≤ 1,

where C(n,k) denotes the binomial coefficient.

Deduce that |F|≤C(n,floor(n/2)).

Finally, classify all antichains F for which equality holds in this cardinality bound:

• If n is even, prove that equality is possible only when F consists of all subsets of size n/2.

• If n is odd, prove that equality is possible only when F consists of all subsets of size (n−1)/2, or all subsets of size (n+1)/2.

Your proof must be self-contained. In particular, justify the counting behind the displayed inequality, and do not merely cite a named theorem.
steps.reference:
Write S_n for the set of all n! permutations (x1,...,xn) of [n]. Every permutation determines the maximal chain of its initial sets

∅ ⊂ {x1} ⊂ {x1,x2} ⊂ ... ⊂ {x1,...,xn}=[n].

Because F is an antichain, this chain contains at most one member of F.

For a fixed set A⊆[n] of size k, count the permutations for which A occurs as an initial set, meaning that A={x1,...,xk}. The first k positions must contain precisely the elements of A, in any of k! orders, and the remaining n−k positions contain the complement [n]\A, in any of (n−k)! orders. Thus exactly

k!(n−k)!

permutations have A as an initial set.

Count pairs (π,A) such that π is a permutation, A∈F, and A is an initial set of π. Counting by A gives

Σ_{A∈F} |A|!(n−|A|)!.

Counting by π gives at most n!, since each permutation's initial-set chain contains at most one member of F. Therefore

Σ_{A∈F} |A|!(n−|A|)! ≤ n!.

Dividing by n! and using

|A|!(n−|A|)!/n! = 1/C(n,|A|)

gives

Σ_{A∈F} 1/C(n,|A|) ≤ 1.

Now let B=C(n,floor(n/2)). The binomial coefficients are largest in the middle: indeed,

C(n,k+1)/C(n,k)=(n−k)/(k+1),

which is at least 1 exactly when k≤(n−1)/2. Hence C(n,k)≤B for every k. Consequently, for every A∈F,

1/C(n,|A|) ≥ 1/B.

Applying the inequality already proved,

1 ≥ Σ_{A∈F} 1/C(n,|A|) ≥ |F|/B.

Thus |F|≤B=C(n,floor(n/2)).

It remains to classify equality cases. Suppose |F|=B. Then both inequalities in

1 ≥ Σ_{A∈F} 1/C(n,|A|) ≥ |F|/B=1

are equalities. In particular, every summand must equal 1/B; otherwise one summand would be strictly larger than 1/B and the sum would exceed 1. Thus every A∈F has a size k for which C(n,k)=B.

If n=2r is even, the unique k with C(n,k)=B is k=r. Thus every member of F has size r. There are exactly C(2r,r)=B such sets, and F has B members, so F is the entire r-th level: all r-subsets of [n].

Now suppose n=2r+1 is odd. The only sizes having binomial coefficient B are r and r+1. Let

X={A∈F: |A|=r},   Y={A∈F: |A|=r+1}.

Each of the two levels has size B, and |X|+|Y|=B. Since F is an antichain, no set in X is contained in a set in Y.

We show that X and Y cannot both be nonempty. Form a bipartite graph H whose left vertices are all r-subsets of [n], whose right vertices are all (r+1)-subsets, and whose edges are inclusions U⊂V. Every r-subset has degree r+1, because it can be enlarged by any of the r+1 elements outside it. Every (r+1)-subset also has degree r+1, because it has r+1 different r-subsets.

There are no H-edges from X to Y, by the antichain property. Hence every one of the (r+1)|X| edges leaving X ends in the complement of Y among the right vertices. But

|right level minus Y|=B−|Y|=|X|.

Since each right vertex has degree only r+1, these |X| right vertices can receive at most (r+1)|X| edges. Therefore they receive exactly all possible such edges, and every edge incident with a right vertex outside Y comes from X. Equivalently, there are no edges from a left vertex outside X to a right vertex outside Y. Together with the already known absence of edges from X to Y, the graph H splits into two disjoint parts:

X together with (right level minus Y),

and

(left level minus X) together with Y.

If both X and Y are nonempty, then both parts are nonempty, so H would be disconnected.

But H is connected. To see this directly, any two r-subsets P and Q can be joined by repeatedly replacing an element of the current r-subset that is not in Q by an element of Q not currently present. One replacement from U to U−{a}∪{b} corresponds in H to the two-edge path

U ⊂ U∪{b} ⊃ U−{a}∪{b}.

Thus all r-subsets lie in one component. Every (r+1)-subset is adjacent to one of its r-subsets, so all vertices of H lie in that same component. This contradiction proves that X and Y cannot both be nonempty.

Therefore either X is empty, in which case F is all (r+1)-subsets, or Y is empty, in which case F is all r-subsets. These two families are antichains and both have B members, completing the classification.
rubric: Correctly counts permutation-initial-set incidences and derives Σ_{A∈F}1/C(n,|A|)≤1 from the antichain condition.
Correctly deduces the middle-binomial cardinality bound, including justification that the central binomial coefficient is maximal.
Correctly handles equality: unique middle level for even n, and a rigorous argument excluding a mixture of the two middle levels for odd n.

## Part 1: Proving the LYM Inequality

**Setup:** Consider a random maximal chain $\emptyset = C_0 \subset C_1 \subset \cdots \subset C_n = [n]$ where $|C_i| = i$. A maximal chain is determined by a permutation $\pi$ of $[n]$ where $C_i = \{\pi(1), \ldots, \pi(i)\}$. There are $n!$ maximal chains.

**Key counting:** For a fixed set $A$ with $|A| = k$, count maximal chains containing $A$. If $C_k = A$, then:
- The first $k$ elements form $A$: arranged in $k!$ ways
- The remaining $n-k$ elements form $[n]\setminus A$: arranged in $(n-k)!$ ways

So exactly $k!(n-k)!$ maximal chains contain $A$.

**The crucial observation:** Since $F$ is an antichain, no maximal chain can contain two distinct members of $F$. (If $A, B \in F$ with $A \subset B$, they'd lie on the same chain; but $F$ is an antichain, so this never happens.)

Therefore, the sets of chains containing different members of $F$ are disjoint.

**The inequality:** The total number of maximal chains is $n!$, so:
$$\sum_{A \in F} k!(n-k)! \leq n!$$

where $k = |A|$. Dividing by $n!$:
$$\sum_{A \in F} \frac{k!(n-k)!}{n!} = \sum_{A \in F} \frac{1}{\binom{n}{k}} \leq 1$$

This is the LYM inequality.

## Part 2: Deducing $|F| \leq \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$

Since $\binom{n}{k}$ is maximized at $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ (and $k = \lceil n/2 \rceil$), we have $\binom{n}{|A|} \leq \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$ for all $A$.

Thus:
$$1 \geq \sum_{A \in F} \frac{1}{\binom{n}{|A|}} \geq \sum_{A \in F} \frac{1}{\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}} = \frac{|F|}{\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}}$$

Therefore $|F| \leq \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$.

## Part 3: Classifying Extremal Antichains

**Case $n = 2m$ even:**

Equality in $|F| \leq \binom{2m}{m}$ requires equality in both inequalities above.

From the LYM inequality: we need $\sum_{A \in F} 1/\binom{2m}{m} = 1$, so $|F| = \binom{2m}{m}$.

Since $F$ contains exactly $\binom{2m}{m}$ sets of size $m$, and there are exactly $\binom{2m}{m}$ subsets of size $m$ total, we have $F = \binom{[2m]}{m}$.

**Case $n = 2m+1$ odd:**

The maximum binomial coefficient is $\binom{2m+1}{m} = \binom{2m+1}{m+1}$.

For equality in $|F| \leq \binom{2m+1}{m}$:

From the second inequality: we need $\binom{n}{|A|} \in \left\{\binom{n}{m}, \binom{n}{m+1}\right\}$ for all $A \in F$, so $|A| \in \{m, m+1\}$.

From LYM equality: $\sum_{A \in F} 1/\binom{n}{|A|} = 1$.

Let $F_m = F \cap \binom{[n]}{m}$ and $F_{m+1} = F \cap \binom{[n]}{m+1}$, with $a = |F_m|$ and $b = |F_{m+1}|$.

Then: $\frac{a}{\binom{n}{m}} + \frac{b}{\binom{n}{m+1}} = 1$, and we want $a + b = \binom{n}{m} = \binom{n}{m+1}$.

Since $\binom{n}{m} = \binom{n}{m+1}$, let this common value be $N$. Then:
$$\frac{a+b}{N} = \frac{a}{N} + \frac{b}{N} = 1$$

So $a + b = N$. But we also need $a/N + b/N = 1$, which is the same condition. 

Wait — let me recheck: we need $a + b = N$ for cardinality equality, and the LYM gives $\frac{a}{N} + \frac{b}{N} = 1$, i.e., $a + b = N$. These are consistent, but we need to check which pairs $(a,b)$ work.

steps.title: Hamiltonicity from Degree Sums
steps.prompt:
Let G be a finite simple undirected graph on n≥3 vertices. Assume that for every pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices x,y of G,

deg(x)+deg(y)≥n.

Prove, without citing any named theorem, that G contains a Hamiltonian cycle: a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once. Your proof must be self-contained.
steps.reference:
Let P=v1,v2,...,vk be a path with as many vertices as possible. Thus k is the maximum possible number of vertices in a path of G.

First, every neighbor of either endpoint v1 or vk lies on P. For example, if v1 had a neighbor z not on P, then z,v1,v2,...,vk would be a path with k+1 vertices, contradicting the choice of P. The same applies to vk.

We show that the vertices of P form a cycle. There are two cases.

If v1 is adjacent to vk, then
v1,v2,...,vk,v1
is a cycle containing all k vertices of P.

Suppose instead that v1 and vk are nonadjacent. Define two sets of indices in {1,...,k−1}:

A={i : v1 is adjacent to v(i+1)},
B={i : vi is adjacent to vk}.

Because every neighbor of v1 lies on P, and v1 is not adjacent to itself, the neighbors of v1 are exactly among v2,...,vk. Hence |A|=deg(v1). Similarly, |B|=deg(vk). By the hypothesis,

|A|+|B|=deg(v1)+deg(vk)≥n.

But A and B are both subsets of a set of only k−1 indices, and k≤n. Therefore k−1≤n−1. If A and B were disjoint, then

|A|+|B|≤k−1≤n−1,

contradicting |A|+|B|≥n. Thus A∩B is nonempty.

Choose i∈A∩B. Then the edges v1v(i+1) and vivk exist. Consequently,

v1,v2,...,vi,vk,v(k−1),...,v(i+1),v1

is a cycle. It visits each of v1,...,vk exactly once: it goes forward along P from v1 to vi, uses the edge vivk, then goes backward along P from vk to v(i+1), and finally uses the edge v(i+1)v1. Thus G contains a cycle C whose vertex set is exactly the vertex set of P.

It remains to prove that this cycle contains every vertex of G. First note that G is connected. If it were disconnected, choose vertices x and y in two distinct connected components. They are nonadjacent. If their component sizes are p and q, then deg(x)≤p−1 and deg(y)≤q−1, so

deg(x)+deg(y)≤p+q−2≤n−2,

contradicting the assumed lower bound n.

Now suppose that C does not contain every vertex. Since G is connected, there must be an edge uc with c on C and u outside C: take a path from a vertex on C to a vertex outside C and consider its first edge leaving C.

Starting with u, traverse the edge uc and then traverse C from c in either direction, stopping just before returning to c. This gives a path containing u together with every one of the k vertices of C, hence a path with k+1 vertices. This contradicts the maximality of P.

Therefore C contains all n vertices. Hence C is a Hamiltonian cycle.
rubric: Chooses a longest path and correctly proves that its endpoints have no neighbors outside that path.
Correctly constructs a cycle through all vertices of the longest path, including the nonadjacent-endpoints case via an intersection/pigeonhole argument on path indices.
Proves connectivity from the degree-sum condition and uses an edge from the cycle to an outside vertex to contradict maximality of the path.
steps.answer:
I need to prove that G is Hamiltonian given that deg(x) + deg(y) ≥ n for all nonadjacent pairs.

**Step 1: Setup**

Among all longest paths in G, choose P = v₁v₂...vₖ with maximum number of vertices. Let S = {v₁,...,vₖ} be the vertices of P.

**Step 2: v₁ and vₖ have all neighbors in S**

If some neighbor of v₁ were outside S, I could extend P, contradicting maximality. Same for vₖ. So N(v₁) ⊆ S and N(vₖ) ⊆ S.

**Step 3: Finding a cycle on S**

Consider A = {vᵢ : v_{i+1} ∈ N(v₁)} and B = N(vₖ), both subsets of {v₁,...,vₖ}.

If A ∩ B ≠ ∅, say vⱼ ∈ A ∩ B, then vⱼ ∈ N(vₖ) and v_{j+1} ∈ N(v₁). This gives cycle C = v₁v₂...vⱼvₖv_{k-1}...v_{j+1}v₁ containing all of S.

If A ∩ B = ∅, then |A| = |N(v₁)| = deg(v₁) and |B| = deg(vₖ), so |A| + |B| = deg(v₁) + deg(vₖ). Since v₁ and vₖ are endpoints of a longest path, they are nonadjacent (otherwise P extends to a cycle, and if any vertex outside, we get longer path; if not, G = cycle and we're done). Thus deg(v₁) + deg(vₖ) ≥ n.

But A ∪ B ⊆ {v₁,...,vₖ₋₁}, so |A ∪ B| ≤ k-1. Since A ∩ B = ∅:
$$|A| + |B| = |A \cup B| \leq k-1 \leq n-1$$

This contradicts deg(v₁) + deg(vₖ) ≥ n. So A ∩ B ≠ ∅, and we have a cycle C on S.

**Step 4: S = V(G)**

If k < n, some vertex w ∉ S. Since G is connected (minimum degree ≥ n/2 ≥ 1.5, so δ(G) ≥ 2 for n≥3, making G connected), take a shortest path from w to C, say to vertex u ∈ S. This creates a longer path than P, contradiction.

Thus k = n, and C is a Hamiltonian cycle.

steps.title: Nontrivial Pair Designs Have at Least as Many Blocks as Points
steps.prompt:
Let V be a set of v>=2 points, and let B1,...,Bb be distinct subsets of V, called blocks. Assume:

1. No block equals V.
2. Every pair of distinct points of V belongs together to exactly one block.

Prove that b>=v.

Your proof must be self-contained and may not cite any named design-theory result. You may use matrices over the real numbers, but you must explicitly justify the rank or linear-independence fact on which your argument relies.
steps.reference:
For each point x in V, let r_x be the number of blocks that contain x.

First observe that r_x>=2 for every x. Indeed, suppose r_x=1, and let B be the unique block containing x. For every other point y in V, the pair {x,y} must lie in exactly one block. Since B is the only block containing x, it must contain y. This holds for every y in V, so B=V, contrary to assumption 1. Hence r_x>=2.

Form the v by b incidence matrix A over the reals. Its rows are indexed by points x in V, its columns by blocks B_j, and

A_{x,j}=1 if x belongs to B_j, and A_{x,j}=0 otherwise.

Let M=AA^T, a v by v matrix. Its (x,y)-entry counts the blocks containing both x and y:

M_{x,y}=sum_{j=1}^b A_{x,j}A_{y,j}.

Thus, if x=y, then M_{x,x}=r_x. If x!=y, then M_{x,y}=1 by assumption 2. Therefore, for every real vector z=(z_x)_{x in V},

z^T M z
= sum_x r_x z_x^2 + sum_{x!=y} z_x z_y
= sum_x (r_x-1)z_x^2 + (sum_x z_x)^2.

Here the last equality follows because

(sum_x z_x)^2=sum_x z_x^2+sum_{x!=y}z_xz_y.

Since every r_x-1 is positive, if z is nonzero then at least one z_x^2 is positive and hence

z^T M z > 0.

Consequently M is nonsingular. To justify this explicitly, if Mz=0 for some z, then z^TMz=0. But the displayed strict positivity shows this is possible only for z=0. Thus the only solution to Mz=0 is z=0, which is exactly nonsingularity.

We now show that the v rows of A are linearly independent. Suppose a real row vector c satisfies c^T A=0. Multiplying on the right by A^T gives

c^TAA^T=c^TM=0.

Because M is nonsingular, this implies c=0. Hence there is no nontrivial linear relation among the rows of A.

Finally, A has b columns, so each row of A is a vector in R^b. A collection of more than b vectors in R^b cannot be linearly independent: for example, placing them as rows in a matrix and performing Gaussian elimination, each nonzero pivot must occur in a different column, so there can be at most b pivot rows, and hence at most b linearly independent rows. Since A has v linearly independent rows, we must have v<=b.

Therefore b>=v, as required.

steps.answer:
I need to prove that in a pairwise balanced design where no block equals V, we have b ≥ v.

## Setup

Let me define the incidence matrix A: a v × b matrix where A_{ij} = 1 if point i is in block B_j, and 0 otherwise.

## Key Step: Analyzing AA^T

Consider the v × v matrix M = AA^T. The entry M_{ij} equals the number of blocks containing both point i and point j.

- For i ≠ j: M_{ij} = 1 (every pair is in exactly one block)
- For i = j: M_{ii} = r_i, the number of blocks containing point i

So M = J + D, where J is the all-ones matrix and D is diagonal with D_{ii} = r_i - 1.

## Proving A has Full Row Rank

I claim that rank(A) = v, which requires b ≥ v. I'll show M = AA^T is invertible.

**Step 1: Each point is in at least two blocks.**

Since v ≥ 2, take point i and another point j. They're together in exactly one block, so r_i ≥ 1. 

Suppose r_i = 1. Let B_1 be the unique block containing i. For any other point j ≠ i, the pair {i,j} must be in some block. Since r_i = 1, this block must be B_1. So {i,j} ⊆ B_1 for all j, meaning B_1 = V. This violates condition 1.

Therefore **r_i ≥ 2 for all i**, so r_i - 1 ≥ 1 for all i.

**Step 2: M is positive definite (hence invertible).**

For any non-zero vector x ∈ ℝ^v:
$$x^T M x = x^T J x + x^T D x = \left(\sum_i x_i\right)^2 + \sum_i (r_i-1)x_i^2$$

Since r_i - 1 ≥ 1 > 0 for all i, we have:
$$x^T M x \geq \sum_i (r_i-1)x_i^2 \geq \sum_i x_i^2 = \|x\|^2 > 0$$

Thus M is positive definite, hence **invertible**.

**Step 3: Conclude rank(A) = v.**

Since M = AA^T is v × v and invertible:
$$\text{rank}(AA^T) = v$$

But rank(AA^T) ≤ rank(A) ≤ v (since A is v × b).

Therefore **rank(A) = v**.

## Conclusion

Since A is a v × b matrix with rank v, we need at least v columns: **b ≥ v**.

steps.title: Edge-coloring bipartite graphs
steps.prompt:
Let G be a finite simple bipartite graph with bipartition L,R, and let Δ be its maximum vertex degree. Prove that the edges of G can be colored with exactly Δ available colors so that no two edges sharing a vertex receive the same color.

Your proof must be self-contained and may not cite any named matching or edge-coloring theorem. You may temporarily add vertices and may temporarily allow parallel edges, provided you justify why this helps and why the final coloring restricts to a valid coloring of G.

In particular, you must prove the matching fact you use rather than merely naming it.
steps.reference:
If Δ=0, then G has no edges, so the assertion is immediate. Assume Δ≥1.

We first prove a matching lemma.

Lemma. Let H be a finite bipartite graph or bipartite multigraph with bipartition X,Y. Suppose that for every subset S⊆X, its neighbor set N(S)⊆Y satisfies |N(S)|≥|S|. Then H has a matching covering every vertex of X.

Proof of lemma. Choose a matching M having as many edges as possible. Suppose, for contradiction, that some vertex of X is unmatched.

Starting from all unmatched vertices of X, form sets Z⊆X and W⊆Y as follows. Put every unmatched vertex of X in Z. A vertex y∈Y is put in W if there is an alternating path from an initially unmatched vertex of X to y which starts with an edge outside M; a vertex x∈X is put in Z if it is an initial unmatched vertex or can be reached by continuing such a path across an edge of M from a vertex of W. Equivalently, paths move from X to Y along nonmatching edges and from Y to X along matching edges.

We claim that N(Z)=W. Certainly W⊆N(Z), because every vertex put in W is reached from a vertex of Z by an edge. Conversely, take z∈Z and an edge zy. If zy is not in M, then an alternating path reaching z can be extended through zy, so y∈W. If zy is in M, then z is not one of the initial unmatched vertices. Any alternating path that reaches z from Y reaches it across its unique matching edge, which must be zy; hence y already belongs to W. Thus every neighbor of Z lies in W, proving N(Z)=W.

No vertex of W is unmatched. Indeed, if y∈W were unmatched, the alternating path from an unmatched vertex of X to y would begin and end at unmatched vertices. Switching membership in M along this path—adding its nonmatching edges and deleting its matching edges—would still give a matching, but with one more edge than M. This contradicts maximality of M.

Therefore every y∈W has a unique matching partner in Z. These partners are distinct, and none is among the initially unmatched vertices of X. Since there is at least one initial unmatched vertex, this gives |W|<|Z|. But N(Z)=W, contradicting the assumed inequality |N(Z)|≥|Z|. Hence M covers all of X. This proves the lemma.

Now return to G. Let p=|L| and q=|R|, and put N=max(p,q). Add isolated vertices to the smaller side, if necessary, so that both sides have exactly N vertices. Call the resulting bipartite graph G0. It still has maximum degree at most Δ.

We next enlarge G0 to a Δ-regular bipartite multigraph H on these same two parts. For each vertex v, define its deficit to be Δ−deg(v). The total deficit on the left is

Σ_{x∈L}(Δ−deg(x))=NΔ−|E(G0)|,

and the same calculation on the right gives

Σ_{y∈R}(Δ−deg(y))=NΔ−|E(G0)|.

Thus the total deficits on the two sides are equal. As long as some deficit remains, there is a left vertex x with positive deficit and a right vertex y with positive deficit. Add one edge xy, allowing it to be parallel to an already existing edge if necessary. This lowers the total deficit on each side by one. Repeating finitely many times produces a bipartite multigraph H in which every vertex has degree exactly Δ. The original graph G is a subgraph of H.

We claim that every d-regular bipartite multigraph with equally many vertices on its two sides has a perfect matching, for every d≥1. Let its bipartition be X,Y, with every vertex having degree d. For any S⊆X, exactly d|S| edges leave vertices of S, and every such edge ends in N(S). Since each vertex of N(S) has total degree d, the number of these edges is at most d|N(S)|. Hence

d|S|≤d|N(S)|,

so |N(S)|≥|S|. By the lemma, there is a matching covering X. Since |X|=|Y|, that matching has |X| edges and also covers every vertex of Y; it is perfect.

Apply this claim to H, which is Δ-regular. It has a perfect matching M1. Delete the edges of M1. Every vertex loses exactly one incident edge, so the remaining bipartite multigraph is (Δ−1)-regular. It therefore has a perfect matching M2. Continue: after deleting M1,...,Mi−1, the remaining multigraph is (Δ−i+1)-regular, so it has a perfect matching Mi. After Δ steps, every edge of H has been deleted exactly once, and

E(H)=M1 disjoint union M2 disjoint union ... disjoint union MΔ.

Color every edge in Mi with color i. Since Mi is a matching, no two edges of color i share an endpoint. Hence this is a proper edge-coloring of H using the Δ available colors.

Finally, restrict this coloring to the original edges of G. Any two original edges sharing a vertex also shared that vertex in H, so they had different colors in H and still have different colors after restriction. Thus G has a proper edge-coloring using Δ colors.
rubric: Proves, rather than cites, a sufficient matching criterion via a maximum matching and alternating reachable sets, including the strict inequality contradiction.
Correctly regularizes the graph by equalizing the bipartition sizes and adding edges, with a valid equality-of-total-deficits argument; allowing parallel edges is handled consistently.
Shows a regular bipartite multigraph has a perfect matching by edge counting, repeatedly removes perfect matchings, and explains why the resulting coloring restricts to the original simple graph.
steps.answer:
I need to prove that a bipartite graph with maximum degree Δ has edge-chromatic number exactly Δ (Kőnig's line coloring theorem), without citing named theorems.

## Setup

I'll prove this by induction on |E|, showing G has a proper Δ-edge-coloring. The lower bound is clear (any vertex of degree Δ needs Δ colors), so I need to show Δ colors suffice.

## Key Lemma: Regular Bipartite Graphs Have Perfect Matchings

**Lemma:** Every k-regular bipartite graph (k ≥ 1) has a perfect matching.

*Proof:* Let H be k-regular bipartite with parts A, B. First, |A| = |B| since k|A| = |E(H)| = k|B|.

For any S ⊆ A, let N(S) be neighbors of S. The edges from S go to N(S), so k|S| ≤ k|N(S)|, thus |S| ≤ |N(S)|. By Hall's marriage theorem (proved below), a perfect matching exists. ∎

**Hall's Theorem Proof (for completeness):** Suppose G' bipartite with parts X,Y satisfies |N(S)| ≥ |S| for all S ⊆ X, but has no matching covering X. Take a maximum matching M and unmatched vertex x₀ ∈ X. Build alternating tree: vertices reachable by M-alternating paths from x₀. Let S = X ∩ (tree), T = Y ∩ (tree). Every vertex in S\{x₀} is matched to T, so |T| = |S| - 1. But N(S) ⊆ T (otherwise we could extend), so |N(S)| ≤ |S|-1 < |S|, contradiction. ∎

## Main Proof

**Step 1: Extend to a regular bipartite graph.**

Given G with bipartition L,R and max degree Δ, I'll add vertices and edges to create a Δ-regular bipartite graph H containing G.

First, add vertices to make |L| = |R| = n (say). For each vertex v with degree d(v) < Δ, I need to add Δ - d(v) edges incident to v. 

Add edges between low-degree vertices in L and R greedily, maintaining simplicity, until no more edges can be added. If vertices u ∈ L and v ∈ R both have degree < Δ, add edge uv. 

If this gets stuck with some vertices still having degree < Δ, then every such vertex in L has all its possible neighbors (all of R) already at full degree, or vice versa. Since degrees are bounded by Δ, if u ∈ L has d(u) < Δ but can't add edges, then all vertices in R have degree Δ. But then sum of degrees in R equals nΔ, so sum in L equals nΔ, contradicting that u has degree < Δ.

So we can add edges to get a bipartite graph where all degrees are Δ or Δ-1. If any vertex has degree Δ-1, since |L|=|R|, the number of degree-Δ-1 vertices in L and R are equal (equal total degree sums). Pair them up and add a perfect matching between them (this may create a multigraph). 

Now we have a Δ-regular bipartite multigraph H containing G.

**Step 2: Decompose H into perfect matchings.**

By the Lemma, H has a perfect matching M₁. Remove M₁ to get (Δ-1)-regular bipartite multigraph. Repeat: find perfect matching M₂, etc.

This gives H = M₁ ∪ M₂ ∪ ... ∪ M_Δ, a decomposition into Δ perfect matchings.

**Step 3: Restrict to G.**

Color edges of Mᵢ with color i. This is a proper Δ-edge-coloring of H, hence restricts to a proper Δ-edge-coloring of G. ∎

steps.title: Intersecting Uniform Families
steps.prompt:
Let n and k be positive integers with n >= 2k. Let F be a collection of k-element subsets of [n] = {1,2,...,n} such that every two distinct sets in F intersect.

Prove that

|F| <= C(n-1,k-1).

Your proof must be self-contained and may not cite any named theorem. In particular, if you use a shifting/compression operation, define it and prove both that it preserves the number of sets and that it preserves the property that every two sets intersect.
steps.reference:
We prove the claim by induction on n, using compressions.

First define a compression. For 1 <= i < j <= n and a k-set A, define

s_ij(A) = (A minus {j}) union {i} if j is in A, i is not in A;
          A otherwise.

For a family F, define its (i,j)-compression C_ij(F) as follows. Each A in F is replaced by s_ij(A) only when s_ij(A) is not already in F; if s_ij(A) is already in F, retain A instead. Thus

C_ij(F) = {s_ij(A): A in F and s_ij(A) notin F} union {A: A in F and s_ij(A) in F}.

This operation preserves the cardinality of the family. Indeed, a set is changed only to a set that was not initially in F, and two distinct changed sets cannot be mapped to the same set: if s_ij(A)=s_ij(B) is different from both A and B, then both A and B are obtained from that image by replacing i with j, so A=B. Thus replacement gives a one-to-one correspondence between the old members and the new members.

We next prove that compression preserves the intersecting property. Suppose F is intersecting, but C_ij(F) contains disjoint sets A' and B'. At least one of A',B' must be a genuinely changed set, since two unchanged sets are members of F and hence intersect. Without loss of generality, suppose

A' = (A minus {j}) union {i}

for some A in F, where j is in A, i is not in A, and A' is not in F. Since A' and B' are disjoint, B' does not contain i and is disjoint from A minus {j}. Also B' cannot be a genuinely changed set, because every genuinely changed set contains i, whereas A' contains i; hence B'=B is an unchanged member of F.

The original sets A and B must intersect because F is intersecting. But B is disjoint from A minus {j}, so their only possible common element is j. Therefore j is in B. We already know i is not in B. Consider

B* = (B minus {j}) union {i}.

If B* were in F, then B* would be disjoint from A: it avoids j, it avoids A minus {j}, and i is not in A. This would contradict that F is intersecting. Hence B* is not in F. But then the compression would have changed B to B*, contradicting that B was unchanged. This contradiction proves that C_ij(F) is intersecting.

Repeatedly perform any compression C_ij that changes the family. This process terminates: whenever a change occurs, the sum of all elements over all sets in the family strictly decreases, because some j is replaced by a smaller i, while the family size stays fixed. Thus after finitely many steps we obtain an intersecting family F' of k-sets, with |F'|=|F|, having the following stability property:

For every A in F', every i<j, if j is in A and i is not in A, then (A minus {j}) union {i} is also in F'.

It is enough to bound |F'|, so rename F' as F.

We now induct on n. If k=1, an intersecting family of singleton sets has at most one member, and

C(n-1,0)=1,

so the result holds.

For the main base case n=2k, pair every k-subset A of [2k] with its complement [2k] minus A. The two sets in a pair are disjoint, so an intersecting family contains at most one member from each complementary pair. Therefore

|F| <= (1/2) C(2k,k) = C(2k-1,k-1),

where the last equality follows from

C(2k,k) = (2k/k) C(2k-1,k-1) = 2C(2k-1,k-1).

Now assume n>2k and that the result is known for smaller values of n whenever the corresponding inequality between parameters holds.

Split F into two parts according to whether the set contains n. Define

F0 = {A in F: n notin A},

and define a family of (k-1)-sets on [n-1] by

F1 = {A minus {n}: A in F and n in A}.

Clearly,

|F|=|F0|+|F1|.

The family F0 is intersecting, since it is a subfamily of F. It consists of k-subsets of [n-1]. Since n>2k, we have n-1>=2k, so the induction hypothesis gives

|F0| <= C(n-2,k-1).

We claim that F1 is also intersecting. Suppose instead that A,B are disjoint members of F1. Then A union {n} and B union {n} are both in F. Since A and B are disjoint and each has k-1 elements, their union has 2k-2 elements. As n>2k, there exists an element

x in [n-1] minus (A union B).

Because A union {n} belongs to F, contains n, and does not contain x<n, stability under compression implies

A union {x} is in F.

But A union {x} is disjoint from B union {n}: A is disjoint from B, x is not in B, and neither set contains the other's extra element. This contradicts that F is intersecting. Thus F1 is intersecting.

The family F1 consists of (k-1)-subsets of [n-1]. Also

n-1 >= 2(k-1).

Applying induction to F1 gives

|F1| <= C(n-2,k-2).

Consequently,

|F| = |F0|+|F1|
     <= C(n-2,k-1)+C(n-2,k-2)
     = C(n-1,k-1),

by the elementary identity obtained by separating the (k-1)-subsets of [n-1] according to whether they contain n-1. This proves the desired bound.
rubric: Defines a family compression precisely and rigorously proves that it preserves both cardinality and pairwise intersection.
Uses termination of repeated compressions to obtain the needed stability property, and correctly proves that the projected family of sets containing n is intersecting.
Completes a valid induction, including the n=2k complementary-pair base case and the binomial-coefficient recurrence.

I need to prove that an intersecting family of k-element subsets of [n] has size at most $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ when $n \geq 2k$.

## Setup

For a family $\mathcal{F}$ of k-subsets of [n], I'll define a shifting operation and show it preserves both the size and the intersecting property, eventually transforming any intersecting family into one contained in a star (all sets containing a fixed element).

## The Shifting Operation

For $1 \leq i < j \leq n$, define the **(i,j)-shift** $S_{ij}$ as follows:

For a set $A \in \mathcal{F}$:
- If $j \in A$, $i \notin A$, and $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \notin \mathcal{F}$, then $S_{ij}(A) = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$
- Otherwise, $S_{ij}(A) = A$

Define $S_{ij}(\mathcal{F}) = \{S_{ij}(A) : A \in \mathcal{F}\}$.

## Shift Preserves Cardinality

**Claim:** $|S_{ij}(\mathcal{F})| = |\mathcal{F}|$.

**Proof:** I need to show $S_{ij}$ is injective on $\mathcal{F}$. Suppose $S_{ij}(A) = S_{ij}(B)$ for $A, B \in \mathcal{F}$.

**Case 1:** $S_{ij}(A) = A$ and $S_{ij}(B) = B$. Then $A = B$.

**Case 2:** $S_{ij}(A) = A \neq (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$ and $S_{ij}(B) = (B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \neq B$.

Then $j \in B$, $i \notin B$, and $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} = A$. Since $i \in A$ and $j \notin A$, we check if $A$ could have been shifted: for $A$ to be unshifted, either $j \notin A$ (true), or $i \in A$ (true), or $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \in \mathcal{F}$. Since $j \notin A$, the shift condition isn't met, so $S_{ij}(A) = A$ is correct.

Now, $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} = A$, so $B = (A \setminus \{i\}) \cup \{j\}$. For $B$ to be shifted, we need $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} = A \notin \mathcal{F}$? No wait — we need $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \notin \mathcal{F}$. But $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} = A \in \mathcal{F}$, contradiction. So this case is impossible.

**Case 3:** Both $A$ and $B$ get shifted. Then $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} = (B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$, so $A \setminus \{j\} = B \setminus \{j\}$, hence $A = B$.

## Shift Preserves Intersecting Property

**Claim:** If $\mathcal{F}$ is intersecting, so is $S_{ij}(\mathcal{F})$.

**Proof:** Take $A', B' \in S_{ij}(\mathcal{F})$ where $A' = S_{ij}(A)$, $B' = S_{ij}(B)$ for $A, B \in \mathcal{F}$. We know $A \cap B \neq \emptyset$.

**Case 1:** $A' = A, B' = B$. Then $A' \cap B' = A \cap B \neq \emptyset$.

**Case 2:** $A' = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$, $B' = B$. 

If $i \in B$, then $i \in A' \cap B'$. 

If $i \notin B$: Since $A \cap B \neq \emptyset$ and $j \notin A'$ (so possibly $j \notin A \cap B$), we have $A \cap B \subseteq (A \setminus \{j\}) \cap B$ or $j \in A \cap B$. 

Actually: $A' \cap B' = ((A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}) \cap B$. Since $i \notin B$, this equals $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cap B$.

If $j \notin A$, then $A' = A$, contradiction. So $j \in A$. If $j \in B$, then since $A \cap B \neq \emptyset$, either there's $x \in (A \setminus \{j\}) \cap B$ (so $A' \cap B' \neq \emptyset$), or $A \cap B = \{j\}$. 

If $A \cap B = \{j\}$: Then $A' = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$, and $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cap B = \emptyset$. But $A'$ was created, so $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \notin \mathcal{F}$. 

Now check: does $A' \cap B' = \emptyset$? We have $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cap B = \emptyset$ and $i \notin B$. So $A' \cap B = \emptyset$. 

But wait — I need to verify this case can happen. Actually, let me recheck: if $A \cap B = \{j\}$, then $A' \cap B = \emptyset$. This seems problematic. Let me recheck the shift condition.

For $A$ to shift: need $j \in A$, $i \notin A$, and $A' = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \notin \mathcal{F}$.

But actually, I need to check if $B$ could equal $A'$. If $B = A'$, then $A' \in \mathcal{F}$, contradicting that $A$ shifts. So $B \neq A'$.

Actually, let me verify: could $A' \cap B = \emptyset$? We need $A \cap B = \{j\}$, $i \notin B$, and $i \notin A$ (true by shift condition). 

Consider: does $B$ shift? If $B$ shifts to $B' = (B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$, then $B' \neq A'$ (since $A' \cap B = \emptyset$ means $i \notin B$, so $B'$ contains $i$ where $A'$ contains elements of $A \setminus \{j\}$). Actually $A' = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$.

If $B$ doesn't shift: $B' = B$, and $A' \cap B = \emptyset$. This is bad!

Wait — I need to recheck. If $A \cap B = \{j\}$, then $j \in B$. For $B$ to not shift, either $j \notin B$ (false), or $i \in B$, or $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \in \mathcal{F}$.

So if $i \notin B$ and $(B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \notin \mathcal{F}$, then $B$ shifts.

So if $i \notin B$ and $B$ doesn't shift, then $C = (B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \in \mathcal{F}$.

Now $A \cap C$: we have $A \cap B = \{j\}$, so $(A \setminus \{j\}) \cap (B \setminus \{j\}) = \emptyset$. Thus $A \cap C = (A \cap (B \setminus \{j\})) \cup (A \cap \{i\}) = \emptyset$ (since $i \notin A$). 

But $A, C \in \mathcal{F}$, contradiction! So if $i \notin B$, then $B$ must shift.

**Case 2 revised:** $A' = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$, $B' = B$, and $i \notin B$. Then $B$ shifts, so this case doesn't occur.

**Case 3:** $A' = A$, $B' = (B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$. Symmetric to Case 2.

**Case 4:** Both shift: $A' = (A \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$, $B' = (B \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\}$. Then $i \in A' \cap B'$.

## The Shifted Family

Apply all shifts $S_{ij}$ for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$ repeatedly until no shift changes the family. Call the result $\mathcal{G}$. Then $\mathcal{G}$ is **shifted**: if $j \in G$, $i \notin G$, $i < j$, then $(G \setminus \{j\}) \cup \{i\} \in \mathcal{G}$.

## Structure of Shifted Intersecting Families

**Claim:** If $\mathcal{G}$ is shifted and intersecting with $n \geq 2k$, then $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \{G : 1 \in G\}$.

**Proof:** Suppose $G \in \mathcal{G}$ with $1 \notin G$. Let $G = \{a_1, \ldots, a_k\}$ with $2 \leq a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k$.

Consider $H = \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$. If $H \in \mathcal{G}$, then since $\mathcal{G}$ is intersecting, $G \cap H \neq \emptyset$, so some $a_i \leq k$.

Actually, let me use a different approach. Define the **shadow** or use a direct argument.

For $G \in \mathcal{G}$ with $1 \notin G$, consider $G' = [k] = \{1, \ldots, k\}$. I'll show $G' \in \mathcal{G}$ leads to contradiction if $G \cap G' = \emptyset$ is possible, but need more care.

Standard argument: For $G \in \mathcal{G}$ with $1 \notin G$, repeatedly replace elements by smaller ones to get $\{2, 3, \ldots, k+1\}$? No, we want to reach $[k]$.

Actually: starting from $G$, shift maximally: replace $a_k$ by $k$, then $a_{k-1}$ by $k-1$, etc. Since $a_i \geq i+1 \geq 2$, we can shift to get $[k] \in \mathcal{G}$.

Now if $G \cap [k] = \emptyset$, then $a_1 > k$, so $G \subseteq \{k+1, \ldots, n\}$. Since $n \geq 2k$, we have $|\{k+1, \ldots, n\}| = n-k \geq k$, so such $G$ exists potentially.

steps.prompt:
Let p be a prime, and let A,B be nonempty subsets of the field F_p of integers modulo p. Define

A+B = {a+b : a in A, b in B}.

Prove that

|A+B| >= min(p, |A|+|B|-1).

Your proof must be self-contained and may not cite any named sumset theorem or polynomial theorem. You may use polynomials over F_p, but if you use an interpolation or coefficient argument, state and prove the precise lemma you need.
steps.reference:
Write r=|A| and s=|B|.

We prove
|A+B| >= min(p,r+s-1).

First suppose r+s>p. We show A+B=F_p. Fix any c in F_p. Consider the two subsets A and c-B={c-b:b in B} of F_p. They have sizes r and s. Since r+s>p=|F_p|, they cannot be disjoint. Hence some a in A and b in B satisfy a=c-b, so c=a+b belongs to A+B. Since c was arbitrary, A+B=F_p, and therefore |A+B|=p, as required.

It remains to consider the case r+s<=p. We prove |A+B|>=r+s-1 by contradiction.

We need the following coefficient lemma.

Lemma. Let X,Y be finite subsets of a field, with |X|=r and |Y|=s. Let P(x,y) be a polynomial of total degree at most r+s-2. Then

[x^(r-1)y^(s-1)]P = sum_{u in X} sum_{v in Y} P(u,v)/(g_X'(u)g_Y'(v)),

where

g_X(z)=product_{u in X}(z-u),

g_Y(z)=product_{v in Y}(z-v),

and [x^(r-1)y^(s-1)]P denotes the coefficient of x^(r-1)y^(s-1).

Proof of the lemma. First establish a one-variable fact. If X has r distinct elements and h(z) has degree at most r-1, then

[z^(r-1)]h(z)=sum_{u in X} h(u)/g_X'(u).

Indeed, for each u in X define

L_u(z)=product_{w in X, w!=u}(z-w)/(u-w).

Then L_u(w)=1 when w=u and 0 when w is another element of X. Thus the polynomial
sum_{u in X}h(u)L_u(z)
has degree at most r-1 and agrees with h at all r points of X. Their difference has degree at most r-1 and has r distinct roots, so it is the zero polynomial. Therefore
h(z)=sum_{u in X}h(u)L_u(z).
The coefficient of z^(r-1) in L_u is
1/product_{w in X,w!=u}(u-w)=1/g_X'(u),
which proves the one-variable fact.

In particular, for an integer i with 0<=i<=r-1,

sum_{u in X}u^i/g_X'(u)=0 if i<r-1,
and this sum is 1 if i=r-1.

Now write P(x,y)=sum c_{ij}x^iy^j. The right-hand side in the lemma equals

sum c_{ij}(sum_{u in X}u^i/g_X'(u))(sum_{v in Y}v^j/g_Y'(v)).

For a monomial with i+j<=r+s-2, a nonzero contribution is possible only if i>=r-1 and j>=s-1: otherwise one of the displayed one-variable sums is zero. But i+j<=r+s-2 then forces i=r-1 and j=s-1. That monomial contributes exactly c_(r-1,s-1). Hence the whole expression is exactly [x^(r-1)y^(s-1)]P. This proves the lemma.

Return to A and B. Assume for contradiction that

|A+B|<=r+s-2.

Because r+s<=p, we have r+s-2<=p-2. Thus we may choose a set D contained in F_p such that

A+B subseteq D and |D|=r+s-2.

Define

P(x,y)=product_{d in D}(x+y-d).

This polynomial has total degree r+s-2. For every a in A and b in B, the element a+b belongs to A+B and hence to D. Therefore one factor in P(a,b) is zero, so

P(a,b)=0 for every (a,b) in A times B.

By the coefficient lemma, this implies

[x^(r-1)y^(s-1)]P=0.

On the other hand, because P depends only on x+y and has degree r+s-2, its coefficient of x^(r-1)y^(s-1) is

binom(r+s-2,r-1).

This element is nonzero in F_p. Indeed, r+s-2<p, so every integer from 1 through r+s-2 is nonzero modulo p. Consequently the factorial formula

binom(r+s-2,r-1)=(r+s-2)!/((r-1)!(s-1)!)

is a quotient of nonzero elements of F_p, hence is nonzero. This contradicts the preceding conclusion that the coefficient is zero.

Therefore |A+B| cannot be at most r+s-2, and so |A+B|>=r+s-1 when r+s<=p. Combining this with the first case gives

|A+B|>=min(p,r+s-1),
as required.

## Lemma (Polynomial Interpolation)

Let $\mathbb{F}$ be a field and $S_1, \ldots, S_n \subseteq \mathbb{F}$ with $|S_i| = d_i + 1$. Let $P(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ be a polynomial with $\deg_{x_i}(P) \leq d_i$ for each $i$. If $P$ vanishes on $S_1 \times \cdots \times S_n$, then $P \equiv 0$.

**Proof:** By induction on $n$. For $n=1$: a univariate polynomial of degree $\leq d_1$ with $d_1+1$ roots is identically zero.

For the inductive step, write:
$$P(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{j=0}^{d_n} P_j(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}) x_n^j$$

For each fixed $(a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}) \in S_1 \times \cdots \times S_{n-1}$, the univariate polynomial in $x_n$ has $d_n+1$ roots (all of $S_n$), so all coefficients are zero. g_X(u)=∏_{x∈X}(u-x),   g_Y(v)=∏_{y∈Y}(v-y),   g_Z(w)=∏_{z∈Z}(w-z).

Let P(u,v,w)∈F[u,v,w] have total degree at most r+s+t−3. Prove the identity

[u^(r−1)v^(s−1)w^(t−1)]P
=
∑_{x∈X}∑_{y∈Y}∑_{z∈Z} P(x,y,z)/(g_X'(x)g_Y'(y)g_Z'(z)).

Here [u^(r−1)v^(s−1)w^(t−1)]P denotes the coefficient of that monomial, and derivatives are formal derivatives over F.

You must prove every interpolation or coefficient fact you use. Deduce in particular that if P vanishes at every point of X×Y×Z, then the coefficient [u^(r−1)v^(s−1)w^(t−1)]P is zero.

$$L(u,v,w) = \sum_{x\in X}\sum_{y\in Y}\sum_{z\in Z} \frac{g_X(u)}{(u-x)g_X'(x)} \cdot \frac{g_Y(v)}{(v-y)g_Y'(y)} \cdot \frac{g_Z(w)}{(w-z)g_Z'(z)}$$

satisfies: for any polynomial $P$ with $\deg_u < r, \deg_v < s, \deg_w < t$:
$$P(u,v,w) = \sum_{x,y,z} P(x,y,z) \cdot \frac{g_X(u)}{(u-x)g_X'(x)} \cdot \frac{g_Y(v)}{(v-y)g_Y'(y)} \cdot \frac{g_Z(w)}{(w-z)g_Z'(z)}$$

**Proof of Lemma 6:** Both sides are polynomials with $\deg_u < r, \deg_v < s, \deg_w < t$ (the right side because each factor $\frac{g_X(u)}{(u-x)}$ has degree $r-1$, etc.). They agree on $X\times Y\times Z$ since at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$, all terms vanish except $(x,y,z)=(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ where the product equals 1. By the uniqueness of interpolation polynomials in each variable, they're equal. ∎

**Lemma 7:** For $P$ with $\deg_u < r, \deg_v < s, \deg_w < t$:
$$[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]P = \sum_{x,y,z}\frac{P(x,y,z)}{g_X'(x)g_Y'(y)g_Z'(z)}$$

**Proof:** Apply Lemma 6. By Lemma 2, $[u^{r-1}]\frac{g_X(u)}{u-x} = 1$, and similarly for $v,w$. So the coefficient of $u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}$ in each product is $\frac{1}{g_X'(x)g_Y'(y)g_Z'(z)}$. ∎

## Final Step: Reduction to Low Degree

**Lemma 8:** If $P$ has total degree $\leq r+s+t-3$, then there exists $\tilde{P}$ with $\deg_u(\tilde{P})<r, \deg_v(\tilde{P})<s, \deg_w(\tilde{P})<t$ such that:
- $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]P = [u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]\tilde{P}$
- $P(x,y,z) = \tilde{P}(x,y,z)$ for all $(x,y,z) \in X\times Y\times Z$

**Proof:** Reduce $P$ modulo $g_X(u)$, $g_Y(v)$, $g_Z(w)$. Specifically:
- Write $P = g_X \cdot Q_1 + R_1$ where $\deg_u(R_1) < r$
- Write $R_1 = g_Y \cdot Q_2 + R_2$ where $\deg_v(R_2) < s$  
- Write $R_2 = g_Z \cdot Q_3 + \tilde{P}$ where $\deg_w(\tilde{P}) < t$

Then $\tilde{P} \equiv P \pmod{g_X, g_Y, g_Z}$, so $\tilde{P}(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)$ on $X\times Y\times Z$.

For the coefficient: note $\deg(g_X) = r$, so $g_X$ has no $u^{r-1}$ term with nonzero coefficient of $v^{s-1}w^{t-1}$ in a way that contributes... actually I need to check this more carefully.

Since $\deg(g_X) = r$, we have $[u^{r-1}]g_X = 0$ (the $u^{r-1}$ coefficient of $g_X$ is $-\sum x$). Actually $g_X = u^r - (\sum x)u^{r-1} + \cdots$.

So $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}](g_X \cdot Q_1)$: if $g_X = u^r - e_1 u^{r-1} + \cdots$, then $g_X \cdot Q_1$ has $u$-degree $\geq r$. The $u^{r-1}$ coefficient comes from $-e_1 u^{r-1} \cdot (\text{coeff of } u^0 \text{ in } Q_1) + u^r \cdot (\text{coeff of } u^{-1} \text{ in } Q_1) = -e_1 [u^0]Q_1$.

Hmm, this is getting messy. Let me use a cleaner argument.

**Cleaner Proof of Lemma 8:** Note that $u^r \equiv e_1 u^{r-1} - e_2 u^{r-2} + \cdots \pmod{g_X(u)}$ where $e_i$ are elementary symmetric polynomials in $X$.

When we replace $u^r$ by lower degree terms, we change coefficients of monomials with $u$-degree $\geq r$. The monomial $u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}$ is unchanged because:
- If a monomial has $u$-degree $\geq r$, after reduction it becomes a sum of monomials with $u$-degree $< r$, so the original $u^{r-1}$ coefficient is unaffected.

Wait — I need to be more careful. The reduction $u^r \to$ (lower terms) can create $u^{r-1}$ terms from higher $u$-degree terms.

Actually, use this: the space of polynomials with $\deg_u<r, \deg_v<s, \deg_w<t$ forms a complete set of representatives for $F[u,v,w]/(g_X(u), g_Y(v), g_Z(w))$. 

For any monomial $u^a v^b w^c$ with $a \geq r$: when reduced, it becomes a polynomial where all monomials $u^{a'}v^{b'}w^{c'}$ satisfy $a' < r$. If $a > r$, then $a' \leq a-1 < a$. 

Crucially: if $a+b+c \leq r+s+t-3$ and $a \geq r$, then after reduction, any resulting monomial has $a' + b' + c' \leq a+b+c - 1 \leq r+s+t-4$ (roughly). 

Actually, the key insight: $u^r \equiv$ (stuff of $u$-degree $< r$) mod $g_X$. So $u^{r+k} \equiv$ (stuff of $u$-degree $< r+k$, but when reduced mod $g_X$, degree $< r$).

For the specific coefficient $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]$: consider that $g_X(u) = u^r + \text{(lower)}$. So $u^r = g_X(u) + \tilde{g}(u)$ where $\deg(\tilde{g}) < r$.

When we reduce $P$ by replacing $u^r \to \tilde{g}(u)$, we subtract $g_X(u) \cdot [u^{\geq r}]P$. This changes coefficients, but note that $g_X(u)$ is divisible by... no wait.

Let me verify: if $P = u^r \cdot Q$, then after reduction $\tilde{P} = \tilde{g} \cdot Q$. The coefficient $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]$ in $u^r Q$ vs $\tilde{g} Q$: if $\deg(Q) = d$, then $u^r Q$ has terms with $u$-degree $\geq r$, while $\tilde{g}Q$ has $u$-degree $< r+d$. 

Actually, I claim: **if total degree of $P$ is $\leq r+s+t-3$, then $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]P$ is unchanged by reduction mod $(g_X, g_Y, g_Z)$.**

Proof: The reduction only affects monomials where $a \geq r$ or $b \geq s$ or $c \geq t$. 

- If $a \geq r$ and $a+b+c \leq r+s+t-3$: after reducing $u^a$, we get terms with $u$-degree $< r$, so $u$-degree drops by at least 1. The new total degree is at most $a+b+c - 1 \leq r+s+t-4$. 

- Can such a reduced term equal $u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}$? It would need $u$-degree exactly $r-1$, $v$-degree $s-1$, $w$-degree $t-1$, total $r+s+t-3$. But we said total degree $\leq r+s+t-4$. Contradiction!

Similarly for reductions in $v$ or $w$. So the coefficient $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]$ is invariant under reduction. ∎

## Conclusion

By Lemma 8, we can replace $P$ by $\tilde{P}$ with $\deg_u < r, \deg_v < s, \deg_w < t$ without changing either side of the desired identity:
- Left side: $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]P = [u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]\tilde{P}$ by invariance
- Right side: $P(x,y,z) = \tilde{P}(x,y,z)$ on $X\times Y\times Z$

By Lemma 7 applied to $\tilde{P}$:
$$[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]\tilde{P} = \sum_{x,y,z}\frac{\tilde{P}(x,y,z)}{g_X'(x)g_Y'(y)g_Z'(z)} = \sum_{x,y,z}\frac{P(x,y,z)}{g_X'(x)g_Y'(y)g_Z'(z)}$$

This proves the identity.

**Corollary:** If $P$ vanishes on $X\times Y\times Z$, then every term in the sum is zero, so $[u^{r-1}v^{s-1}w^{t-1}]P = 0$. ∎

steps.title: Finite-field common-zero divisibility
steps.prompt:
Let p be prime and let f_1,...,f_m be polynomials in F_p[x_1,...,x_n], where n>=1. Assume that

deg(f_1)+...+deg(f_m)<n,

where deg denotes total degree. Let N be the number of vectors a in F_p^n such that

f_1(a)=f_2(a)=...=f_m(a)=0.

Prove that p divides N.

Your proof must be self-contained. In particular, you may use basic facts about a field, but you must prove every finite-field power-sum fact and every polynomial-degree fact needed in your argument; do not cite any named theorem.
steps.reference:
We work in the field F_p. All equalities below are in F_p unless explicitly described as integer counts.

First prove two elementary facts.

Fact 1. If c is a nonzero element of F_p, then c^(p-1)=1.

Proof. Multiplication by c permutes the p-1 nonzero elements of F_p. Therefore

product_{u in F_p, u != 0} u = product_{u in F_p, u != 0} cu = c^(p-1) product_{u in F_p, u != 0} u.

The product on the left is nonzero, so it may be cancelled, giving c^(p-1)=1.

Fact 2. For every integer e with 0 <= e < p-1,

sum_{u in F_p} u^e = 0.

Proof. If e=0, then the sum is p, which is 0 in F_p.

Now suppose 1 <= e < p-1. The polynomial T^e-1 has degree e, so it cannot have more than e roots in a field: indeed, each distinct root contributes a distinct linear factor, and a nonzero polynomial of degree e cannot be divisible by more than e such factors. Since F_p^* has p-1>e elements, there is some c in F_p^* for which c^e != 1.

Multiplication by c permutes F_p, so

sum_{u in F_p} u^e = sum_{u in F_p} (cu)^e = c^e sum_{u in F_p}u^e.

Thus (c^e-1) sum_{u in F_p}u^e=0. Since c^e-1 is nonzero, the sum is 0.

Now define, for a in F_p^n,

I(a)=product_{i=1}^m (1-f_i(a)^(p-1)).

By Fact 1, if f_i(a) is nonzero then f_i(a)^(p-1)=1, and if f_i(a)=0 then f_i(a)^(p-1)=0. Hence the factor 1-f_i(a)^(p-1) equals 1 exactly when f_i(a)=0 and equals 0 otherwise. Consequently,

I(a)=1 if f_1(a)=...=f_m(a)=0,
I(a)=0 otherwise.

Therefore, as an element of F_p,

N = sum_{a in F_p^n} I(a).

It remains to prove that this sum is zero in F_p.

Expand the polynomial

Q(x_1,...,x_n)=product_{i=1}^m (1-f_i(x_1,...,x_n)^(p-1)).

Every monomial occurring in Q has total degree strictly less than (p-1)n. Indeed, choosing the 1 term from every factor gives the constant monomial. Any other term is obtained by choosing f_i^(p-1) from some nonempty subset S of the factors, and its total degree is at most

(p-1) sum_{i in S} deg(f_i) <= (p-1) sum_{i=1}^m deg(f_i) < (p-1)n.

Write Q as a finite sum of monomials:

Q(x_1,...,x_n)=sum_alpha c_alpha x_1^(alpha_1)...x_n^(alpha_n).

For every exponent vector alpha occurring here, alpha_1+...+alpha_n < (p-1)n. Hence at least one coordinate, say alpha_j, satisfies alpha_j<p-1; otherwise every alpha_j would be at least p-1 and the total degree would be at least (p-1)n.

For such a monomial, summing over all of F_p^n factors as

sum_{a in F_p^n} a_1^(alpha_1)...a_n^(alpha_n)
= product_{j=1}^n (sum_{u in F_p}u^(alpha_j)).

The factor corresponding to the coordinate with alpha_j<p-1 is zero by Fact 2. Thus the sum over F_p^n of every monomial of Q is zero. By linearity,

sum_{a in F_p^n} Q(a)=0.

Since Q(a)=I(a), this says N=0 in F_p. The ordinary integer N is therefore congruent to 0 modulo p. Hence p divides N.
rubric: Correctly constructs an indicator for simultaneous zeros using the factors 1-f_i(a)^(p-1), including a self-contained justification that nonzero elements of F_p have (p-1)-st power 1.
Proves the required power-sum vanishing for all exponents 0<=e<p-1, including the e=0 case and a valid justification for choosing an element c with c^e!=1 when e>0.
Expands the indicator polynomial and rigorously uses the total-degree bound to show every monomial has some variable exponent below p-1, so its sum over F_p^n vanishes and therefore N is 0 modulo p.
steps.answer:
I need to prove that $p$ divides $N$, the number of common zeros of $f_1, \ldots, f_m$ in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$.

## Setup

Let $S = \{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n : f_1(a) = \cdots = f_m(a) = 0\}$, so $N = |S|$.

I'll use the indicator function approach. For $t \in \mathbb{F}_p$, define:
$$\delta(t) = 1 - t^{p-1}$$

**Claim 1:** For $t \in \mathbb{F}_p$, we have $\delta(t) = 1$ if $t = 0$, and $\delta(t) = 0$ if $t \neq 0$.

*Proof:* If $t = 0$, then $\delta(0) = 1 - 0 = 1$. If $t \neq 0$, then by Fermat's little theorem, $t^{p-1} = 1$, so $\delta(t) = 1 - 1 = 0$. ∎

Therefore, the indicator of $S$ is:
$$\mathbf{1}_S(a) = \prod_{j=1}^m \delta(f_j(a)) = \prod_{j=1}^m \left(1 - f_j(a)^{p-1}\right)$$

And:
$$N = \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} \mathbf{1}_S(a) = \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} \prod_{j=1}^m \left(1 - f_j(a)^{p-1}\right)$$

## The Key Reduction

Expand the product:
$$\prod_{j=1}^m \left(1 - f_j^{p-1}\right) = \sum_{T \subseteq \{1,\ldots,m\}} (-1)^{|T|} \prod_{j \in T} f_j^{p-1}$$

For each subset $T$, let $g_T = \prod_{j \in T} f_j^{p-1}$ (where $g_\emptyset = 1$). Then:
$$N = \sum_{T \subseteq \{1,\ldots,m\}} (-1)^{|T|} \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} g_T(a)$$

## Power Sum Lemma

**Lemma:** Let $h \in \mathbb{F}_p[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ with $\deg(h) < n(p-1)$. Then $\sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} h(a) = 0$.

*Proof:* By linearity, it suffices to prove this for monomials $h = x_1^{e_1} \cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with $e_1 + \cdots + e_n < n(p-1)$.

We have:
$$\sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} a_1^{e_1} \cdots a_n^{e_n} = \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\sum_{a_i \in \mathbb{F}_p} a_i^{e_i}\right)$$

So I need: if $0 \leq e < p-1$, then $\sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p} a^e = 0$.

**Sub-lemma:** For $0 \leq e \leq p-2$: $\sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p} a^e = 0$.

*Proof:* Let $S_e = \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p} a^e$. For $e = 0$: $S_0 = \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p} 1 = p \cdot 1 = 0$ in $\mathbb{F}_p$.

For $1 \leq e \leq p-2$: Let $g$ be a generator of $\mathbb{F}_p^*$ (which is cyclic of order $p-1$). Then:
$$S_e = \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^*} a^e = \sum_{k=0}^{p-2} g^{ke} = \frac{g^{e(p-1)} - 1}{g^e - 1}$$

Since $e \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p-1}$, we have $g^e \neq 1$, so the denominator is nonzero. Since $g^{p-1} = 1$, the numerator is $1 - 1 = 0$. Thus $S_e = 0$. ∎

Now for the monomial: if $e_1 + \cdots + e_n < n(p-1)$, then some $e_i < p-1$. For that $i$, we have $\sum_{a_i \in \mathbb{F}_p} a_i^{e_i} = 0$ (either by the sub-lemma if $e_i \leq p-2$, or if $e_i = 0$). Thus the product is zero. ∎

## Applying the Lemma

For $T \neq \emptyset$: 
$$\deg(g_T) = \sum_{j \in T} (p-1)\deg(f_j) \leq (p-1)\sum_{j=1}^m \deg(f_j) < (p-1)n = n(p-1)$$

So by the Lemma, $\sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} g_T(a) = 0$ for all $T \neq \emptyset$.

For $T = \emptyset$: we have $g_\emptyset = 1$, so $\sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} g_\emptyset(a) = p^n \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

Therefore:
$$N = \sum_{T \subseteq \{1,\ldots,m\}} (-1)^{|T|} \sum_{a \in \mathbb{F}_p^n} g_T(a) \equiv p^n + \sum_{\emptyset \neq T} (-1)^{|T|} \cdot 0 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$$

Thus **$p$ divides $N$**. ∎
steps.steering_note: The candidate is competent on standard combinatorial arguments but has shown serious gaps in controlling polynomial-degree arguments, so this probes whether they can execute a clean finite-field counting proof from first principles.

steps.title: Vertex-disjoint paths and separators
steps.prompt:
Let G be a finite simple undirected graph, and let s and t be distinct vertices. An s-t separator is a set S⊆V(G)\{s,t} such that deleting all vertices of S (and all incident edges) leaves no path from s to t. Prove that the maximum number of s-t paths having pairwise disjoint internal vertices equals the minimum size of an s-t separator.

Your proof must be self-contained. You may use a flow-style argument, but then you must define flows, residual networks, and augmenting paths, and prove the max-flow/min-cut fact needed in your proof rather than citing any named theorem.
steps.reference:
Let n=|V(G)|, and put q=n. We prove that the two quantities in the statement are equal.

First, if P1,...,Pr are s-t paths with pairwise disjoint internal vertices, and S is an s-t separator, then every Pi contains an internal vertex of S. Indeed, after S is deleted, no Pi can remain an s-t path. Since the paths have disjoint internal vertices, these required vertices of S are distinct. Thus r≤|S|. Consequently,

maximum number of internally disjoint s-t paths ≤ minimum separator size.   (1)

It remains to prove the reverse inequality.

Construct a directed capacitated network D as follows. For every vertex v∈V(G)\{s,t}, create two vertices vin and vout and an arc vin→vout of capacity 1. Keep s and t unsplit. For every undirected edge {u,v} of G, add the two directed arcs corresponding to each direction: from uout to vin and from vout to uin, where s is used in place of sin and sout, and t is used in place of tin and tout. Give every such arc capacity q. Thus, for example, if {s,v} is an edge, add s→vin and vout→s, each of capacity q.

A flow in a directed capacitated network with source s and sink t is an assignment f(e) of a nonnegative real number to every arc e such that f(e)≤c(e), where c(e) is its capacity, and such that at every vertex other than s,t, the total flow entering equals the total flow leaving. Its value is the total flow leaving s minus the total flow entering s. We shall use only integral flows.

We now prove the needed flow fact.

Flow lemma. In any finite directed network with nonnegative integral capacities, there is an integral flow whose value equals the minimum capacity of an s-t cut.

Here an s-t cut is a partition (X,V\X) with s∈X and t∉X. Its capacity is the sum of capacities of all arcs directed from X to V\X.

Proof of the flow lemma. Start with the zero flow. Given an integral flow f, its residual network has, for every original arc a→b of capacity c and current flow f(a→b), a forward residual arc a→b of residual capacity c-f(a→b), if this is positive, and a backward residual arc b→a of residual capacity f(a→b), if this is positive. A residual s-t path is a directed path from s to t in this residual network.

If there is such a path, let d be the smallest residual capacity on its arcs. Since capacities and the current flow are integral, d is a positive integer. Increase the flow by d on every original arc used forward along the path, and decrease it by d on every original arc whose backward residual arc is used. The resulting assignment is again a feasible integral flow: capacity bounds hold by the definition of residual capacity, and at every internal vertex of the path the added and removed amounts balance. Its value rises by d.

Repeat while an s-t residual path exists. This process stops, because each augmentation raises the nonnegative integral flow value by at least 1, while the value is bounded above by the finite total capacity of arcs leaving s.

Let f be the resulting flow, and let X be the set of vertices reachable from s in the final residual network. Then s∈X and t∉X. If an original arc a→b has a∈X and b∉X, its forward residual capacity is zero, so f(a→b)=c(a→b). If an original arc a→b has a∉X and b∈X, its backward residual capacity is zero, so f(a→b)=0.

Sum flow conservation over all vertices of X except s. All flow on arcs having both ends in X cancels. This gives

value(f) = Σ_{a∈X,b∉X} f(a→b) - Σ_{a∉X,b∈X} f(a→b).

The preceding observations make the first sum the capacity of the cut (X,V\X), and the second sum zero. Hence value(f) equals the capacity of this cut.

On the other hand, every flow has value at most the capacity of every s-t cut: summing conservation over the source side of a cut gives value(f) equal to flow leaving that side minus flow entering it, which is at most the total capacity of arcs leaving it. Therefore f has value equal to the minimum cut capacity. This proves the lemma.

Apply the lemma to D, and let λ be the value of a maximum integral flow. We next show that λ is the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths in G.

Because the flow is integral, repeatedly follow an arc carrying positive flow starting at s. At any encountered vertex other than t, flow conservation guarantees that if positive flow has entered then some positive-flow arc leaves. Since the network is finite, this procedure reaches t after deleting any directed cycles that arise. It yields an s-t directed path along which at least one unit of flow can be removed. Repeating decomposes the flow into λ directed s-t paths, together with possibly some directed cycles; cycles may simply be discarded. Every directed s-t path in D corresponds, after contracting each pair vin,vout back to v, to an s-t walk in G, and deleting repeated portions gives an s-t path in G.

Each internal vertex v of G can occur in at most one of these λ paths, because every use of v requires the arc vin→vout, whose capacity is 1. Thus these λ paths have pairwise disjoint internal vertices. Therefore the maximum number of such paths in G is at least λ.

Conversely, the first observation (1), or directly sending one unit along each transformed path in D, shows that no family of internally disjoint paths can have more than λ members. Hence λ is exactly the maximum number of internally disjoint s-t paths.

Finally, we show that λ is also the minimum separator size. Let S be any s-t separator. Let R be the set of vertices reachable from s in G−S. Form a cut X in D as follows: include s; for every v∈R\{s}, include both vin and vout; and for every v∈S, include vin but not vout. Put all remaining network vertices outside X. There is no capacity-q arc from X to its complement. Indeed, such an arc would correspond to an edge of G from a vertex reachable from s in G−S to a vertex outside R∪S, contradicting the definition of R; arcs into vin for v∈S do not cross because vin was placed in X. The only arcs from X to its complement are vin→vout for v∈S, each of capacity 1. Thus this cut has capacity |S|. By the flow lemma, λ≤|S| for every separator S.

For the converse direction, take a minimum cut (X,V\X) in D, of capacity λ. There are at most n−1 internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths in G: aside from a possible direct edge st, every such path uses at least one distinct vertex of V(G)\{s,t}. Hence λ≤n−1<q. Since every non-vertex arc has capacity q, no capacity-q arc crosses this minimum cut. Let

S={v∈V(G)\{s,t}: vin∈X and vout∉X}.

The cut capacity is therefore |S|=λ. We claim S separates s from t in G. If not, let s=v0,v1,...,vk=t be an s-t path in G−S. It yields a directed route in D from s to t. Starting in X and ending outside X, this route must contain an arc crossing from X to its complement. It cannot be a capacity-q arc, as none such crosses the cut. Therefore it must be some vin→vout, which says vi∈S, contradicting that the original path avoids S. Thus S is an s-t separator of size λ.

So the minimum separator size is both at least and at most λ. It equals λ, which also equals the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths. This proves the result.
rubric: Proves the easy inequality by showing that every separator must meet each internally disjoint path in distinct internal vertices.
Gives a correct self-contained augmenting-path proof of the integral max-flow/min-cut lemma, including residual arcs, termination, and the reachable-set cut.
Correctly performs vertex splitting, converts integral flow into internally vertex-disjoint paths, and converts a minimum cut back into a separator while handling the large-capacity arcs.
steps.answer:
I need to prove that the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths equals the minimum size of an s-t separator. This is Menger's theorem. I'll use a flow-based approach, building everything from scratch.

## Setup: Vertex-Splitting and Flow Network

First, convert the vertex-disjoint paths problem to an edge-disjoint paths problem. Create a directed graph $G'$ from $G$:

- For each vertex $v \in V(G) \setminus \{s,t\}$, create two vertices $v_{in}$ and $v_{out}$ connected by a directed edge $(v_{in}, v_{out})$ with capacity 1.
- For each edge $\{u,v\} \in E(G)$ with $u,v \notin \{s,t\}$, add directed edges $(u_{out}, v_{in})$ and $(v_{out}, u_{in})$ with capacity $\infty$ (or a large number, say $|V(G)|$).
- For edges involving $s$ or $t$: if $\{s,v\} \in E(G)$, add edge $(s, v_{in})$ with capacity $\infty$; if $\{t,v\} \in E(G)$, add edge $(v_{out}, t)$ with capacity $\infty$.

**Key observation:** A flow of value $k$ in $G'$ corresponds to $k$ internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths in $G$, and vice versa. The capacity-1 edges $(v_{in}, v_{out})$ enforce that each internal vertex is used at most once.

## Definitions

**Flow:** A function $f: E(G') \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ satisfying:
- **Capacity constraint:** $f(e) \leq c(e)$ for all edges $e$
- **Conservation:** For all $v \notin \{s,t\}$: $\sum_{u:(u,v)\in E} f(u,v) = \sum_{w:(v,w)\in E} f(v,w)$

The **value** of flow $f$ is $|f| = \sum_{v:(s,v)\in E} f(s,v) - \sum_{u:(u,s)\in E} f(u,s)$ (net flow out of $s$).

**s-t Cut:** A partition $(A,B)$ of $V(G')$ with $s \in A$, $t \in B$. Its **capacity** is $c(A,B) = \sum_{e=(u,v): u\in A, v\in B} c(e)$.

## The Max-Flow/Min-Cut Theorem (for integral capacities)

**Theorem:** $\max\{|f| : f \text{ is a flow}\} = \min\{c(A,B) : (A,B) \text{ is an s-t cut}\}$.

**Proof:**

*Step 1: Weak duality.* For any flow $f$ and cut $(A,B)$:
$$|f| = \sum_{\substack{u\in A, v\in B \\ (u,v)\in E}} f(u,v) - \sum_{\substack{u\in A, v\in B \\ (v,u)\in E}} f(v,u) \leq \sum_{\substack{u\in A, v\in B \\ (u,v)\in E}} c(u,v) = c(A,B)$$

So max-flow ≤ min-cut.

*Step 2: Residual network and augmenting paths.* For flow $f$, define **residual capacity** $c_f(u,v) = c(u,v) - f(u,v) + f(v,u)$ (capacity minus forward flow plus backward flow). The **residual graph** $G_f$ contains edge $(u,v)$ if $c_f(u,v) > 0$.

An **augmenting path** is an s-t path in $G_f$. If such a path exists, we can augment: let $\delta = \min\{c_f(e) : e \text{ on path}\} > 0$. Increase flow by $\delta$ on forward edges, decrease by $\delta$ on backward edges. This preserves conservation and increases $|f|$ by $\delta$.

*Step 3: Termination and optimality.* Since all capacities are integers (or $\infty$), we can maintain integral flows. The finite-capacity edges have capacity 1, so we can augment at most $|V(G)|$ times before saturating all vertex-capacity edges. Thus the process terminates with flow $f^*$ where $G_{f^*}$ has no s-t path.

*Step 4: Extracting a minimum cut.* Let $A = \{v \in V(G') : \text{path from } s \text{ to } v \text{ in } G_{f^*}\}$, and $B = V(G') \setminus A$. Then $(A,B)$ is an s-t cut (since $t \notin A$).

For any edge $(u,v)$ with $u \in A, v \in B$: we have $c_f(u,v) = 0$, so $f^*(u,v) = c(u,v)$ and $f^*(v,u) = 0$. Thus:
$$|f^*| = \sum_{u\in A, v\in B} f^*(u,v) - \sum_{u\in A, v\in B} f^*(v,u) = \sum_{u\in A, v\in B} c(u,v) = c(A,B)$$

Combined with weak duality, $f^*$ is maximum and $(A,B)$ is minimum.

## Connecting Back to the Original Problem

**Claim:** The max number of internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths equals the max flow value in $G'$.

*Proof:* Given $k$ such paths in $G$, send flow 1 along each corresponding path in $G'$ (using the capacity-1 edges for internal vertices). This gives flow value $k$. Conversely, any integral flow decomposes into paths using each capacity-1 edge at most once, giving $k$ vertex-disjoint paths.

**Claim:** The min s-t separator size equals the min cut capacity in $G'$.

*Proof:* Given an s-t separator $S$ in $G$, the cut $(A,B)$ where $A = \{s\} \cup \{v_{in}, v_{out} : v \notin S, \text{ reachable from } s \text{ in } G-S\}$ has capacity $|S|$ (cutting exactly the $|S|$ capacity-1 edges for vertices in $S$). Conversely, any finite cut must cut only capacity-1 edges (since $\infty$ edges are too expensive), and the corresponding vertices form an s-t separator.

## Conclusion

By max-flow/min-cut: 
$$\max(\text{internally vertex-disjoint } s\text{-}t \text{ paths}) = \max\text{-flow} = \min\text{-cut} = \min(\text{s-t separator size})$$

This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

steps.title: Symmetric Chain Partition
steps.prompt:
For n>=0, call a chain in the subset lattice 2^[n] a sequence A_r ⊂ A_{r+1} ⊂ ... ⊂ A_q such that |A_i|=i for every i. Call it symmetric if r+q=n.

Prove, by induction on n, that 2^[n] can be partitioned into pairwise disjoint symmetric chains.

Then use your partition to prove that every antichain F⊆2^[n] satisfies

|F| <= C(n, floor(n/2)).

Your proof must explicitly describe how to turn a symmetric-chain partition of 2^[n-1] into one of 2^[n], and must verify both that the new chains are symmetric and that they partition every subset of [n] exactly once.
steps.reference:
We prove the symmetric-chain partition statement by induction on n.

For n=0, 2^[0] consists only of the empty set. The one-term chain (empty set) is symmetric, since its sole set has size 0 and 0+0=0. Thus the statement holds.

Now assume that 2^[n-1] has been partitioned into pairwise disjoint symmetric chains. Consider one such chain. Write it as

A_r ⊂ A_{r+1} ⊂ ... ⊂ A_{n-1-r},

where |A_i|=i. It is symmetric in 2^[n-1], so its first and last ranks satisfy r+(n-1-r)=n-1.

From this old chain construct chains in 2^[n] as follows. Let

C_1: A_r ⊂ A_{r+1} ⊂ ... ⊂ A_{n-1-r} ⊂ A_{n-1-r}∪{n}.

If r<=n-2-r, equivalently r<n-1-r, also form

C_2: A_r∪{n} ⊂ A_{r+1}∪{n} ⊂ ... ⊂ A_{n-2-r}∪{n}.

If r=n-1-r, then C_2 is empty and is simply omitted.

Each displayed sequence is a chain: the inclusions among the A_i are strict, and adjoining the fixed element n preserves strict inclusion. Also, the final inclusion in C_1 is strict because n is not in A_{n-1-r}, as that set belongs to [n-1].

The chain C_1 starts at rank r and ends at rank n-r, because |A_{n-1-r}∪{n}|=n-r. Thus its endpoint ranks sum to

r+(n-r)=n,

so C_1 is symmetric in 2^[n].

When C_2 is nonempty, it starts at rank r+1 and ends at rank n-1-r. Its endpoint ranks sum to

(r+1)+(n-1-r)=n,

so C_2 is also symmetric in 2^[n].

We now verify that C_1 and C_2 partition exactly the subsets arising from the old chain. The subsets in C_1 not containing n are precisely

A_r,A_{r+1},...,A_{n-1-r}.

The subsets in C_1 containing n consist only of A_{n-1-r}∪{n}. The subsets in C_2, when it exists, are precisely

A_r∪{n},A_{r+1}∪{n},...,A_{n-2-r}∪{n}.

Therefore C_1 together with C_2 contains exactly one copy of A_i and exactly one copy of A_i∪{n} for every i from r through n-1-r. No set is repeated: the sets without n are distinct from those with n, and among the sets with n the indices i are distinct.

Apply this construction separately to every chain in the assumed partition of 2^[n-1]. Every subset S of [n] belongs exactly once in the resulting chains. Indeed:

- If n is not in S, then S is a unique subset of [n-1], hence belongs to exactly one old chain and appears in that old chain's C_1.
- If n is in S, write S=A∪{n}, where A⊆[n-1]. The set A belongs to exactly one old chain. If A is the top set of that chain, then S appears as the final set of C_1. Otherwise it appears in C_2.

Thus the new chains are pairwise disjoint and cover 2^[n]. This completes the induction.

Now let F be an antichain in 2^[n]. In any chain, any two distinct sets are comparable by inclusion. Hence a chain contains at most one member of F. Therefore

|F| <= (number of chains in a symmetric-chain partition of 2^[n]).

It remains to count the chains. Put m=floor(n/2).

If n=2m is even, every symmetric chain has endpoint ranks r and 2m-r. Since r<=m<=2m-r, it contains exactly one set of size m. Since the chains partition all subsets, assigning to each chain its unique m-set gives a bijection between the chains and the m-subsets of [n]. Hence the number of chains is C(n,m).

If n=2m+1 is odd, every symmetric chain has endpoint ranks r and 2m+1-r. It contains exactly one set of size m, and also exactly one set of size m+1. Again, since the chains partition the lattice, assigning each chain its unique m-set gives a bijection between the chains and the m-subsets of [n]. Hence the number of chains is C(n,m).

In either case, the number of chains is C(n,floor(n/2)). Consequently,

|F| <= C(n,floor(n/2)),

as required.
rubric: Gives the correct inductive construction from each old chain, including the second chain and the condition under which it is empty.
Proves that the constructed chains are symmetric and that, across all old chains, every subset of [n] occurs exactly once.
Correctly derives the antichain bound by counting chains through their unique middle-rank set(s).
